art.text: Aksumite builders made most palaces, villas, houses, churches and monasteries from alternating layers of stone and wood. The protruding wooden support beams were named "monkey heads" and became a staple of Aksumite architecture. They also mark Aksumite influence in later structures.

Aksumite builders carved stelae (hawilts) and later entire churches out of single blocks of rock. Among the most spectacular survivals are the giant stelae, one of which, now fallen, is the single largest monolithic structure ever erected or attempted to be erected. Scholars think it may have fallen during or right after its erection.

Ethiopian tradition dates the origins of zema, its sacred music, to the 6th century. It credits Yared with composing the liturgical hymns and an indigenous system of musical notation called meleket. Music in Ethiopia is divided between secular music (zafan) and sacred music (zema).

Ethiopian crosses of wood and metal are usually copper alloy or brass, plated with gold or silver. Their flat cast heads carry elaborate openwork decoration, and many incorporate curved motifs called the "arms of Adam". Except in recent Western-influenced examples, they usually have no figure of Christ.

The introduction of Islam in Somalia's early medieval era brought architectural influences from the Arabian Peninsula and Persia. Builders shifted from drystone to coral stone, sundried bricks and widespread use of limestone. Many new designs such as mosques were built on the ruins of older structures.
The monastery of Debre Damo, dating from the 6th century, is given as a good example of still-standing Aksumite architecture.

Aksumite influence remained strongest in the early medieval, or Late Aksumite, period and again under the Zagwe. Carving of churches from rock was emulated in Tigray, mainly in the 10th and 11th centuries. Around Lalibela the same tradition peaked mainly in the 12th century.

Muslim religious figures introduced Islam to northeastern Ethiopia in the 7th century, and to the coasts of neighboring Somalia in the 8th century. Since the 7th century Islamic artistic traditions have developed in Ethiopia alongside Christian ones. Ethiopia's main artistic expressions include architecture, painting, goldsmithing and manuscript illuminations.

Large underground tombs, often located beneath stelae, are among Aksum's monumental structures. Well-known monolithic tombs include the "Tomb of the False Door" and the tombs of Kaleb and Gebre Mesqel in Axum.
Rock-hewn churches first appeared in the late Aksumite era and reached their peak under the Zagwe. The architecture of the Zagwe, seen at Lalibela, shows a connection to earlier Aksumite traditions.

Some of the oldest known structures in Somalia are burial cairns called taalo. They are found throughout the country and the wider Horn of Africa, with many similar structures at Haylan, Qa'ableh, Qombo'ul, El Ayo, Damo, Maydh and Heis. Many remain unexplored.

Somali shrines honoring patriarchs and forefathers evolved from ancient Somali burial customs. In northern Somalia the tombs mainly feature domes and square plans, while in southern Somalia the preferred medieval style was the pillar tomb.

war.text: At its height, the Kingdom of Aksum spanned what is now Eritrea, northern Ethiopia, eastern Sudan, Yemen and southern Saudi Arabia. By the 7th century it had begun a slow decline that brought extreme loss of territory. Aksum was among the nations hit by the first plague pandemic, the Ethiopian Highlands received less rainfall, and the destruction of stelae from this time suggests internal unrest. This "Post-Aksumite Period" lasted until the Zagwe dynasty took power.

In the late 10th century, the Kingdom of Aksum fell to a queen known as Gudit. Historians are unsure of her ethnicity and religion, but she is theorized to have been Agaw and likely non-Christian, as she targeted churches in her attacks. She is said to have ended the Aksumite era by force.

Late 10th-century external documents describe a queen ruling "al-Ḥabaša" (Abyssinia), and one calls her queen of the "Bani al-Hamwiyah". The documents say she killed the king of Ethiopia, and suggest she had seized power as early as the 960s. She is known as Gudit.

Gudit was certainly non-Christian, and her reign was characterized by the destruction of churches in Ethiopia. This is seen as opposition to the spread of Christianity in the region. During the 10th century the Ethiopian church had also gone many years without a metropolitan sent from Alexandria.

Tradition states that during Islam's inception, coalitions of the Banu Makhzum and the Umayyads quarreled in Ifat. The area is thought to be connected to the Arab migration of the lineage of Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, who feared reprisals after the Assassination of Ali the caliph. Ifat was a Muslim region of the Horn of Africa, on the eastern edge of Shewa.

literature.text: The oldest surviving Ge'ez manuscript is the Garima Gospels, which dates to the 5th or 6th century. Ge'ez is the language of the ancient Axumite texts of Ethiopia and Eritrea.

The roots of Ethiopian historical writing go back to the ancient Kingdom of Aksum, which lasted until about 940. Its early texts were written in the Ge'ez script or the Greek alphabet. They appeared as manuscripts and as inscriptions on monumental stelae and obelisks that documented contemporary events.

The decline of Aksum was followed by a long dry spell in writing. From the 7th to the 13th century, a time marked by political instability, little new literary work was produced in Ethiopia. Ge'ez literature only entered its most productive period after the Solomonic dynasty was established in 1270.

The legend of the queen Gudit, who is traditionally believed to have overthrown the Kingdom of Aksum in the 10th century, is found in a 13th-century chronicle by the monk Tekle Haymanot. He compiled historical writings gathered from various Ethiopian churches and monasteries. The chronicle says that after being exiled from Axum she married a Jewish king of Syria and converted to Judaism.

The 10th-century sheikh Ishaaq bin Ahmed is a semi-legendary figure who is known only from Somali oral traditions and Arabic hagiologies. Tradition says he crossed from Arabia to the Horn of Africa in the 10th or 11th century and settled at Maydh. Scholars disagree over how historical these accounts are.

One legend holds that Dil Na'od, the last king of Aksum, kept his daughter Mesobe Werq in isolation because of a prophecy that her son would overthrow him. She eloped with the nobleman Mara Takla Haymanot from Lasta. He eventually killed the Aksumite king in a duel, took the throne and founded the Zagwe dynasty.

In the late 9th century the Arab Muslim scholar and traveler Al-Yaqubi wrote about the Horn of Africa. He described the Kingdom of Adal as a small wealthy kingdom whose headquarters was Zeila. He noted that the kingdom dated back to the beginning of that century.

The tradition crediting Yared with the hymns and the notation is doubted. A 16th-century royal chronicle credits two clerics with the notation system instead. Zema is also part of Beta Israel culture, while the attribution to Yared and the notation system are not, which suggests Yared was not responsible for these creations.

politics.text: In the late 10th century, a queen known as Gudit ruled over the land of al-Ḥabaša. External documents state that she killed the king of Ethiopia. She was certainly non-Christian, since her reign was characterized by the destruction of churches in Ethiopia, seen as opposition to the spread of Christianity in the region.

The Kingdom of Aksum had been a powerful empire, but by the 7th century it had begun a slow decline. This "Post-Aksumite Period" saw extreme loss of territory and lasted until the Zagwe dynasty rose to power. Several political, economic and ecological reasons have been proposed for the decline.
In the 6th century Aksum conquered South Arabia, though it struggled to maintain control there. It also began to gradually lose its dominance over Red Sea trade to Persians and Arabians.

In the late 10th century the Kingdom of Aksum fell to a queen known as Gudit. External documents state that she killed the king of Ethiopia, and suggest she had seized power at least as early as the 960s. Her reign was marked by the destruction of churches, which is seen as opposition to the spread of Christianity in the region.
By the 9th century, Muslim Sultanates were being established in the Horn of Africa. Islam then spread slowly through much of the continent by trade and preaching.

External documents from the late 10th century describe a queen ruling the land of "al-Ḥabaša" (Abyssinia). One calls her queen of the "Bani al-Hamwiyah" and says she killed the king of Ethiopia. They suggest she had seized power at least as early as the 960s.

Three inscriptions found in Axum name two Christian kings, Dabra Ferem and his son Hasani Dan'el, who are not recorded on Ethiopian regnal lists. Their reigns likely fell in the early 10th century, when the power of the Solomonic line was in decline. Enno Littmann theorized they were forerunners of the Zagwe dynasty.

Fatagar was founded during the arrival of Islam in Eastern Ethiopia in the early 10th century. It was one of several confederates of Zeila, alongside Adal, Ifat, Shewa, Mora and Dawaro, and it later separated Muslim and Christian dominions in the Horn.

Historians are unsure of Gudit's ethnicity and religion. She is theorized to have been Agaw and likely non-Christian, since she targeted churches in her attacks. Confusion surrounds the period directly after her reign.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church was subordinate to the Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria. During the 10th century, Alexandria had not sent it a metropolitan for many years. Gudit's reign left the church in a deteriorated situation.
One inscription tells how Hasani Dan'el attacked rebel tribes in Kassala. It claims that he conquered thirty peoples.
A third inscription says Hasani Dan'el went to Axum after his campaigns to be acknowledged as king. There he imprisoned the old king.

A second inscription says the people of Welkait rebelled and laid waste to Axum. In response, Hasani Dan'el carried off large numbers of their cattle and other animals. He then went to the country of the Maya and took 10,000 sheep and 3,000 cattle.

Tradition states that at Islam's inception the Banu Makhzum and Umayyad coalitions quarreled in Ifat, on the eastern edge of Shewa. Centuries later, the Walasma dynasty overthrew the Makhzumi dynasty there.

According to Harar chronicles cited by Enrico Cerulli, a 10th century Somali saint called "Aw" Barkhadle was the fifth ancestor of the founder of the Walashma dynasty. Some Walashma rulers are thought to be buried at the site of Aw-Barkhadle in modern-day Somaliland. The dynasty's success was said to be due to this descent.

After Gudit's reign ended, the succeeding Ethiopian king reached out to Pope Philotheos of Alexandria about the church's deteriorated situation. Philotheos re-established relations between Egypt and Ethiopia. This set the scene for a Christian renaissance in Ethiopia.

philosophy.text: Africa was the first continent Islam reached from the Middle East, in the early 7th century CE. In May 614 CE, Muhammad told a number of his early disciples, who were facing persecution by the polytheistic inhabitants of Mecca, to seek refuge across the Red Sea in the Christian Kingdom of Aksum, in present-day Eritrea and Ethiopia. The article says these were likely the earliest Muslims in Africa, and links their flight to local dissatisfaction with Muhammad in Mecca.
Christian monasticism has been practiced in Ethiopia since the Aksumite era in the 6th century AD. The Nine Saints, who came from the Byzantine Empire, played a crucial role in developing it.

Ethiopian philosophy arises from the confluence of Greek and Patristic philosophy with traditional Ethiopian modes of thought. Besides oral tradition, it was preserved early in written form through Ge'ez manuscripts.
Christianity survived the decline of the Kingdom of Aksum in the seventh century. It continued through the Dark Age, when written records began to overshadow external sources.

Gudit, a queen who is said to have killed the king of Ethiopia, ruled in a reign marked by the destruction of churches. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church had gone many years in the 10th century without a metropolitan sent from Alexandria. After Gudit's reign ended, the succeeding king appealed to Pope Philotheos of Alexandria about the deteriorated situation, and Philotheos re-established relations between Egypt and Ethiopia. This set the scene for a Christian renaissance.

Because of its early isolation from Byzantium and Alexandria, the sources of its Christian spirituality, Ethiopia received some of its philosophical heritage through Arabic versions. Its moral reflection of religious inspiration favored narrative, parable, apothegm and rich imagery over abstract argument.

culture.text: Ethiopian tradition traces coffee drinking back to Kaldi, a 9th century goat herder from Keffa Zone. He noticed his goats dancing uncontrollably after eating a certain shrub, and he picked its berries.

Early Ethiopian monasticism was similar to that of neighboring regions such as Egypt, Nubia, and the Levant. As in Egypt, it is unlikely that Ethiopian monasteries played an active role in the Christianization of the local population.

Christianity persisted through the Early Middle Ages in Ethiopia, and many large church buildings were constructed in the northern provinces. These were followed by rapid changes in material culture, such as coinage and funerary traditions.

Islam reached the Horn of Africa from the Arabian Peninsula shortly after the Hijrah. Zeila's Masjid al-Qiblatayn, with its two mihrabs, dates to the 7th century and is one of the oldest mosques in the world.

In the story, Kaldi was advised to show the berries to priests in a nearby monastery. One monk called Kaldi's generosity "the Devil's work" and tossed the berries into the fire. The delicious odor that followed led to the birth of coffee.
